# Daily Papers
The project automatically fetches the latest papers from arXiv based on keywords.

The subheadings in the README file represent the search keywords.

Only the most recent articles for each keyword are retained, up to a maximum of 100 papers.

You can click the 'Watch' button to receive daily email notifications.

Last update: 2026-10-20

| **[FuTransformer: FP8 prefill and INT4 decode for Llama-style inference on Hopper]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23796v1)** | 2026-10-16 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Transformer prefill reuses weights across tokens and is dominated by matrix multiplication and activation data movement; single-token decode has limited reuse and is dominated by weight and KV-cache reads. We present FUTRANSFORMER, a CUDA implementation of a Llama-style Transformer block for NVIDIA Hopper GPUs. It applies CODA's GEMM-plus-epilogue approach to inference, adding direct KV-cache placement, folding the fixed RMSNorm gain into weights, writing FP8 output directly with delayed scaling, and supporting prefill without padding. Decode uses INT4 projection weights and an INT4 KV-cache copy. Weights and keys follow Tensor Core fragment layouts for direct dequantization into MMA operands without full intermediate tiles. A block-diagonal Hadamard transform reduces cache quantization error from outlier channels. On one H100, prefill is up to 1.48x faster than compiled PyTorch FP8 and reaches 1.29 PFLOP/s. For gate/up projection with SwiGLU at the 8B shape, our BF16 path is 1.13x faster than CODA. Our FP8 path is 2.02-2.18x faster than the evaluated BF16 CODA path. Across 8B and 70B shapes at batches 1-32, INT4 decode is 1.3-2.4x faster than the faster of PyTorch's BF16 and INT4 blocks at each point: 2.1-3.3x faster than compiled, CUDA-graphed BF16 and 1.3-6.3x faster than the same block using PyTorch's INT4 projection kernel, which targets a single query row and loses to BF16 at batch 32. It is also 31-51% faster than our FP8 path. Complete Llama-3.1-8B decode takes 2.8 ms per step at batch one, versus 8.1 ms for the compiled transformers implementation. Decoding every WikiText-2 token through the INT4 weight path raises perplexity from 6.24 to 7.23 with round-to-nearest weights or 6.99 with GPTQ in the same format; the rotated INT4 cache adds 0.20. The kernels match a quantized reference computation within 0.001 perplexity.</p></details> |  |
| **[DLite: History-free Speculative Decoding for Agentic AI]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23787v1)** | 2026-10-16 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Speculative decoding has become a mainstream technique for accelerating large language model (LLM) inference by using a lightweight draft model to generate candidate tokens that are subsequently verified by the target model. However, agentic workloads introduce long and continuously evolving contexts and frequent multi-turn interactions. Under such workloads, we observe that existing draft models suffer from up to an 80% degradation in acceptance length, while maintaining their historical KV cache introduces substantial system overhead. In this paper, we identify the growing historical context as a common source of both problems and introduce DLite, a history-free speculative decoding framework for agentic AI. DLite directly reuses contextual hidden states from the target model and performs local speculative prediction without explicitly maintaining the historical context, transforming an increasingly complex modeling problem into local simple prediction problem. A lightweight sequential head further restores intra-block causal dependencies with low overhead. To effectively train this heterogeneous history-free architecture, we introduce a tailored two-stage training strategy. Experiments on general-purpose, long-context and agentic workloads show that DLite achieves 2-6 acceptance length and outperforms the state-of-the-art speculative decoding method, DSpark, up to 70%.</p></details> | 14 pages, 5 figures |
| **[HBFSim: A Simulator for Exploring HBF in Memory Hierarchies for LLMs]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23503v1)** | 2026-10-16 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>High Bandwidth Flash (HBF) has recently emerged as a promising technology that provides terabyte-scale accelerator-local capacity at bandwidths approaching HBM, with a potential cost-per-bit advantage over HBM. However, its NAND foundation brings long latency, out-of-place updates, and finite write endurance directly into the accelerator memory hierarchy, making its effects on performance and lifetime difficult to predict. To study this emerging design space, we present HBFSim, an LLM-aware event-driven simulator for heterogeneous HBM+HBF memory systems that preserves application-level memory semantics while modeling flash-internal behavior. HBFSim models HBM, HBF with host-managed flash translation, and conventional capacity tiers in one simulation driven by a calibrated serving frontend. Using HBFSim, we study decoding of Llama-3.1-70B and Qwen3-235B-A22B under three workloads that differ in their input and output lengths. HBF serves data that does not fit in HBM 11.0--19.0$\times$ faster than host DRAM; HBM is better used to hold the running sequences' KV cache than as a cache for HBF; and at a published peak load of Llama-3.1-70B, HBF lasts 2.0 to 6.9 years, in proportion to the stacks that share the KV writes. The artifact is available at https://github.com/FlashLabAE/HBFSim and will track public HBF device data as it becomes available.</p></details> |  |
| **[RealtimeWAM: One-Step Asynchronous World Action Models]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06617v2)** | 2026-10-16 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>World Action Models (WAMs) incorporate visual representations from video generation backbones to guide action prediction. Recent efficient WAMs adopt Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architectures and compute video representations once for reuse by the action expert. However, intra-expert iteration (\ie, multi-step action denoising) and inter-expert waiting (\ie, sequential execution of the video and action experts) still limit inference efficiency. To this end, we present RealtimeWAM, an extremely efficient WAM variant with one-step action generation and asynchronous inference, addressing these two bottlenecks. To reduce intra-expert iteration, we propose Teacher-Anchored Consistency Distillation (TACD) to address a local-global error gap: low local consistency error alone does not guarantee accurate final actions. TACD supplements local consistency with explicit supervision from the frozen teacher's multi-step rollout endpoint, enabling accurate one-step action generation. Additionally, we propose Cross-Expert Wavefront Pipelining (CEWP) to eliminate unnecessary expert-level waiting. It overlaps the two experts through block-wise sharing of the video KV cache, synchronizing only immediately before the corresponding action attention consumes it. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks (\eg, LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin) and model variants (\eg, Fast-WAM and Faster-WAM) demonstrate the superiority of RealtimeWAM. Notably, RealtimeWAM maintains near-lossless performance (\ie, $<1\%$ drop) across these benchmarks while delivering significant end-to-end speedup (\eg, $\sim25\times$ on H100). Our code and checkpoints are available via this \href{https://github.com/ModelTC/LightX2V/tree/main/scripts/realtimewam}{link}.</p></details> | <details><summary>The code and checkpoints are available at https://...</summary><p>The code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/ModelTC/LightX2V/tree/main/scripts/realtimewam</p></details> |
| **[OxyGen: Unified KV Cache Management for VLA Inference under Multi-Task Parallelism]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.14371v5)** | 2026-10-16 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Embodied AI agents increasingly require parallel execution of multiple tasks, such as manipulation, conversation, and memory construction, from shared observations under distinct time constraints. Recent Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs) support such heterogeneous outputs, yet existing inference systems incur redundant computation and resource contention when serving concurrent tasks on-device. We identify isolated KV cache management as the root cause. To address this, we propose unified KV cache management, an inference design that treats the KV cache as a first-class shared resource across tasks and control cycles. This abstraction enables two key optimizations: cross-task KV sharing eliminates redundant prefill of shared observations, while cross-frame continuous batching batches unfinished language requests from different frames and advances them within a per-frame decoding budget. We implement this design in OxyGen and evaluate $π_{0.5}$ on NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 and Jetson AGX Thor. OxyGen achieves up to 3.7$\times$ speedup over isolated execution, delivering over 200 tokens/s language throughput and 70 Hz action frequency simultaneously on RTX 4090. We also validate the design on Xiaomi-Robotics-0 and StarVLA across different backbones and expert configurations. We further demonstrate the inference gains on a humanoid robot with on-board Jetson AGX Thor.</p></details> | NeurIPS 2026 |
| **[Prism Attention: Proposal-Refined Index Sharing Mechanism for Efficient LLMs Inference]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22985v1)** | 2026-10-16 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Long-context decoding in large language models (LLMs) is increasingly bottlenecked by the memory and computation required to attend over an ever-growing Key-Value (KV) cache at each autoregressive step. Although token-level sparse attention reduces this burden by restricting computation to a small subset of relevant past tokens, its practical gains are often offset by repeatedly recomputing layer-wise sparse indices as the context grows. A common remedy is to share sparse indices across layers by computing them only at designated anchor layers, but such static reuse ignores the layer-wise evolution of attention patterns, causing the reused indices to progressively deviate from the layer-specific optima and incur substantial attention loss. By revisiting cross-layer sparsity from the perspective of attention dynamics, we find that inter-layer salient token shift is highly localized: although the exact top-$κ$ indices differ across layers, the core high-attention tokens remain stable, with changes concentrated near the expanded boundary of previously selected regions. Motivated by this, we propose Prism Attention, a proposal-refined sparse attention framework. It replaces rigid cross-layer index reuse with a coarse-to-fine strategy, preserving layer-wise adaptability while retaining the efficiency benefits of cross-layer sharing. Extensive experiments show that Prism Attention achieves state-of-the-art performance among mainstream sparse attention methods on both reasoning and long-context benchmarks, while attaining a $3.4\times$ end-to-end decoding speedup over FlashAttention at 128K context length.</p></details> | <details><summary>Published as a main conference paper at NeurIPS 20...</summary><p>Published as a main conference paper at NeurIPS 2026</p></details> |
| **[BS-Spec: BFP-Based Bit-Sharing for Self-Speculative LLM Decoding with LUT-Driven Mixed-Precision Acceleration]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22877v1)** | 2026-10-16 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed across diverse inference services, serving workloads span a wide range of batch sizes, context lengths, and performance requirements. Speculative decoding improves inference throughput, but conventional approaches require a separate draft model and KV cache, while existing self-speculative methods suffer from workload-insensitive draft configurations and inefficient mixed-precision execution. In this paper, we present BS-Spec, a block floating point (BFP)-based bit-sharing framework that jointly optimizes draft construction, workload-aware precision selection, and hardware execution. BS-Spec derives multiple draft representations directly from a single BFP target model by partially loading the most significant bits of weights and the KV cache while preserving shared exponents, eliminating separate draft-model storage. Offline calibration selects the weight and KV-cache precision pair that maximizes estimated speedup for each serving regime, and a precision lookup table applies the selected configuration at runtime. To support this adaptive execution, we design a mixed-precision BFP accelerator with a lookup table (LUT)-based variable-precision datapath for both draft and target computation. Experimental results show that BS-Spec achieves up to $1.9\times$ speedup over conventional autoregressive decoding and improves speedup over the evaluated bit-sharing self-speculative decoding baselines by $67.2\%$ on average, demonstrating the benefits of jointly co-designing bit sharing, precision adaptation, and specialized hardware for diverse LLM serving workloads.</p></details> |  |
| **[Stealthy Poisoning Attacks via Reused KV Cache of Reasoning]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22873v1)** | 2026-10-16 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Modern large language model (LLM) systems reuse key-value (KV) caches to accelerate inference. Recent work has shown that reusing KV caches from reasoning traces can also improve task performance, similar to retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). We demonstrate that this form of KV cache reuse introduces new poisoning vulnerabilities. We propose R$^2$ECAP (Reused Reasoning-Cache Poisoning), a black-box attack that plants poisoned reasoning traces solely through interactions with a system's chat interface. R$^2$ECAP constructs two traces: a preceding trace that steers the model toward an adversarial target and a retained trace that carries this target. Because the retained trace is generated conditioned on the preceding trace, its KV cache preserves residual adversarial influence, even after the preceding trace and its cache entries are discarded. We evaluate R$^2$ECAP on three open-weight LLMs and three datasets. R$^2$ECAP achieves up to 79% attack success rate (ASR) and outperforms HijackKV, a state-of-the-art white-box KV poisoning attack, in 8 of 9 resource-constrained settings. It also achieves 46% ASR in a realistic reasoning-trace retrieval system. Finally, R$^2$ECAP remains stealthy, with only 1% of its retained responses detected by a popular prompt injection detector.</p></details> | 18pages, 2figures |
| **[FuseRAG: Fusing Structure and Evidence into Inference for Cost-Efficient Graph-based RAG]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22818v1)** | 2026-10-16 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) exploits relationships among evidence to support multi-hop question answering. However, conveying retrieved graphs through non-unique linear textual contexts to Large Language Models (LLMs) leads to graph-structure degradation and inefficient KV-cache reuse. Meanwhile, graph-structure order optimization is already NP-hard, and the additional KV-cache reuse objective further complicates the search by introducing potentially conflicting orders. To tackle these issues, we propose FuseRAG, a cost-efficient graph-based RAG framework that shifts most retrieved evidence from explicit textual contexts to latent representations. Our main idea is to separate reusable evidence content from query-aware structural interactions in latent space, while retaining only a few explicit facts as semantic anchors. The resulting latent representations are injected into decoder self-attention, where they reshape attention over evidence and thereby influence hidden states and next-token probabilities. This design preserves graph structure through latent interactions, enables evidence reuse beyond exact token-prefix matching. Experiments on three multi-hop question-answering datasets with Llama-3-8B and Qwen3.5-9B show that FuseRAG improves answer quality while achieving up to 2.7x and 2.2x TTFT speedups over the fastest graph-based baseline, respectively.</p></details> |  |
| **[SAFETYEDIT: Sparse Internal Targets with Prompt-Wide Control for LLM Jailbreak Backdoors]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22640v1)** | 2026-10-15 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Model-editing backdoors aim to induce harmful responses under a trigger while preserving ordinary behavior on untriggered input. Recent model-editing approaches target affirmative response prefixes through rank-one updates to a small subset of model weights. Yet when this prefix-level target is satisfied, the model may still revert to refusal or produce a coherent, apparently compliant response that does not address the request. To overcome this limitation, existing internal-representation approaches shift focus from output tokens to dense, high-dimensional compliance directions in latent space. Existing representation-level approaches rely on preservation constraints to maintain conditionality, motivating us to ask whether a smaller internal target can offer a different effectiveness-preservation trade-off. Motivated by the comparable control capability of single-coordinate interventions, we investigate a sparse refusal-related MLP coordinate as this target. We propose SAFETYEDIT, which optimizes a single refusal-related coordinate and uses KV-cache marking in early attention layers to propagate a prefix-trigger signal across subsequent instruction positions. On some checkpoints a downstream MLP reader converts this signal into control of the coordinate, while on others the propagated signal alone suffices; the method is defined by the sparse target rather than by a fixed writer-reader pair. Across four open-weight LLMs and three dataset groups, SAFETYEDIT achieves the highest triggered Guard ASR in 11 of 12 comparisons and the highest mean StrongREJECT score in all 12, relative to the baselines evaluated for each model. Crucially, comprehensive ablation and behavioral audits confirm generally minimal changes in untriggered behavior and general capabilities in the tested configurations.</p></details> | <details><summary>35 pages,4 figures; includes appendix...</summary><p>35 pages,4 figures; includes appendix</p></details> |
| **[MemLLM: End-to-end In-Storage Acceleration of On-device Retrieval-Augmented Generation using Precomputed KV Caches]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22579v1)** | 2026-10-15 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) on edge devices enables personalized large language model (LLM) inference while preserving privacy. However, RAG's inherent length asymmetry makes the prefill phase the dominant bottleneck. While precomputing the KV caches offline alleviates the prefill cost on server systems, the multi-gigabyte caches over the narrow interconnect create a severe I/O wall for on-device systems. To mitigate this, we propose MemLLM, an end-to-end in-storage processing (ISP) architecture that executes the complete attention pipeline based on precomputed KV caches within the SSD. MemLLM utilizes per-channel accelerators to fully utilize the aggregated NAND channel bandwidth and accelerates all KV cache-related computations on the storage-side to minimize PCIe transfers. To efficiently handle the sparse updates required by RAG, MemLLM introduces a fused recomputation-query kernel paired with a hardware-based filter logic to halve the NAND read volume and eliminate write-back penalties. Furthermore, MemLLM's global SRAM-based stateful reduction engine enables a completely DRAM-less dataflow, thereby removing the internal memory bottlenecks and bounding the PCIe egress to an $O(1)$ footprint. A full-stack software stack allows asynchronous, zero-copy transfers from the ISP to the host and provides transparent execution within modern ML frameworks. Evaluated across eight real-world RAG datasets and six on-device LLM models, MemLLM achieves an average end-to-end speedup of 4.06$\times$ over the GPU baseline.</p></details> | <details><summary>To be published in IEEE/ACM MICRO 2026...</summary><p>To be published in IEEE/ACM MICRO 2026</p></details> |
| **[Velox: Spatial Memory Makes World Models Efficient]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22311v1)** | 2026-10-15 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Video world models turn actions and camera motion into long visual rollouts, making video a natural interface for interactive simulation. Such interaction requires responsive generation, yet coherent rollouts must retain visual memory of what has already been generated. Chunked video diffusion models usually keep this context in growing KV caches, so later chunks become progressively slower. To address this bottleneck, we introduce Velox, a training-free attention router for region-level context selection using frustum slab correspondences from streaming geometry. Velox represents historical blocks as camera frustum slabs with depth intervals and obtains current-block depth through recency-priority multiwarp. For well-covered regions, frustum slab overlap softly modulates each layer's model-derived block importance. Uncovered regions retain the model-derived route without geometric bias. The fixed token-block granularity matches FlashAttention-style tiled execution and reduces the attention term that grows with rollout length. Frustum slab construction runs asynchronously with denoising on the same H200. At chunk 48, Velox accelerates attention by $4.36\times$ and denoising by $2.43\times$. On the full 158-case WBench navigation split, it remains within 0.15 API-free average points of dense LingBot-Fast-Cam. Please see our project page at https://velox-world.com/velox/ for more details.</p></details> |  |
| **[Archer: Adaptive Reuse of Cached Hidden States for Efficient Rollback in Diffusion Language Models]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08086v3)** | 2026-10-15 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Diffusion language models (DLMs) can revise earlier predictions as context evolves, but rollback requires costly full-sequence recomputation. Conventional key-value (KV) caching assumes immutable historical states and is difficult to reconcile with such revision. We introduce Adaptive Reuse of Cached Hidden States for Efficient Rollback (Archer), a training-free caching method for rollback-capable DLMs. Archer recomputes the mutable response at every update while reusing prompt K/V within a bounded response-state neighborhood. This asymmetric boundary amortizes prompt computation without restricting rollback. Bounded reuse also delays feedback from tentative tokens while keeping response revision active. Our analysis characterizes the cache boundary, bounds state-dependent approximation error, and gives a decoder-margin condition for preserving full-refresh decisions. On code-generation benchmarks, Archer achieves the best mean performance of 33.63% with a 2.57x mean speedup, reaching 2.95x speedup on a single benchmark. On non-code benchmarks, Archer achieves up to 4.33x speedup over LLaDA-Confidence while improving average accuracy. Controlled analyses support the delayed prompt feedback mechanism. Our code is available at https://github.com/Hxnng/Archer</p></details> | <details><summary>26 pages, 7 figures, 12 tables; revised manuscript...</summary><p>26 pages, 7 figures, 12 tables; revised manuscript, updated author list and affiliations</p></details> |
| **[Efficient KV Cache Migration for Geo-Distributed LLM Inference in Collaborative Edge Computing]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22172v1)** | 2026-10-15 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown exceptional capabilities but rely heavily on centralized cloud GPU clusters, leading to high bandwidth costs, latency, and privacy issues. Edge computing offers a solution by deploying LLMs closer to users on edge servers, yet single edge servers often cannot meet LLMs' heavy computational demands. Collaborative Edge Computing (CEC) addresses this challenge by integrating resources of multiple geo-distributed heterogeneous edge servers, which jointly host small model shards and associated Key-Value (KV) cache for distributed inference. However, edge servers may disconnect or easily become overloaded, making it essential to migrate stateful KV cache to other servers for ensuring continuous service. Existing cloud-based KV cache management methods, such as direct cross-GPUs transmission and recomputation from input tokens are ill-suited for bandwidth-constrained and resource-limited edge environments. In this work, we propose EdgeFlow, a novel hybrid KV cache migration scheme that integrates direct KV cache transmission with activation-based recomputation, leveraging parallel computation and communication to minimize migration time. On this basis, we formulate a multi-node KV migration optimization problem and design a 2-approximation algorithm based on improved linear programming relaxation and bipartite graph techniques. Extensive experiments on a real-world distributed LLM inference platform demonstrate that EdgeFlow reduces migration time by up to 45%, significantly enhancing the robustness and efficiency of distributed LLM inference in collaborative edge computing.</p></details> | <details><summary>Accepted by ICDCS 2026...</summary><p>Accepted by ICDCS 2026</p></details> |
| **[DropKV: Decoupling Residual-Output Perturbation for Near-Optimal KV-Cache Eviction]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22130v1)** | 2026-10-15 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Key-value (KV) cache management has become a critical bottleneck for scaling Large Language Models (LLMs) to long-context scenarios due to linear memory growth. While recent eviction methods have moved beyond simple attention-score heuristics to incorporate value representations, they typically face a fundamental trade-off: the underlying optimization for minimizing output perturbation is an NP-hard combinatorial problem, leading to mathematically suboptimal heuristics or implementations that are difficult to kernelize. In this work, we propose DropKV, a simple principled eviction framework based on Decoupled Residual-Output Perturbation. By decoupling the joint eviction decision into independent per-token scoring, DropKV circumvents combinatorial intractability and admits a provable constant-factor approximation guarantee under a cone condition that we empirically verify on three long-context LLMs. To ensure practical viability, we provide a high-performance implementation using fused Triton kernels that avoid materializing the full attention matrix, delivering a 19.8x scoring-kernel speedup that translates to up to a 9.9% matched-batch end-to-end prefill speedup. Extensive evaluations on the RULER and LongBench benchmarks demonstrate that DropKV consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines at equivalent cache budgets, achieving the lowest inference latency among eviction methods while also remaining faster than the dynamic cache baseline.</p></details> | <details><summary>Accepted by NeurIPS 2026...</summary><p>Accepted by NeurIPS 2026</p></details> |
| **[PrefixFlow: Training-Time KV Caching for Schedule-Level Prefix Reuse in LLM RL Training]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.01143v4)** | 2026-10-15 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>In reinforcement learning (RL) post-training, one prompt fans out into $N$ trajectories, yet standard trainers replay the shared prefix's forward and backward pass $N$ times; in long-context retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and multimodal workloads, this repetition dominates training compute. Existing designs reuse the prefix within one computation graph (a packed sequence, fused kernel, or tree traversal); under the trainer's memory limits and parallelism, their compute savings do not reliably become shorter steps. We present PrefixFlow, which takes the prefix out of that graph and into the training schedule through a training-time KV cache: Phase A runs one prefix forward and caches its keys and values ($K/V$); Phase B trains suffixes as ordinary microbatches that read only $K/V$ and write back only their gradients ($gK/gV$); Phase C runs one delayed prefix backward on the accumulated $gK/gV$. Memory and parallelism then become manageable: dormant prefix activations are offloaded during Phase B to free high-bandwidth memory (HBM) for suffixes, and context, pipeline, and data parallelism each schedule the phases through a local rule while tensor and expert parallelism need no change, so saved compute becomes shorter steps under any microbatch split. On dense models, and on mixture-of-experts (MoE) models under Rollout Routing Replay, PrefixFlow matches full-sequence training within bfloat16 (BF16) tolerance. Against an identically configured baseline, it speeds up end-to-end verl RL training on a long-prefix RAG workload by $1.90\times$ ($6.1\times$ on the actor update). In controlled sweeps, actor-side speedup grows with prefix ratio and group size, reaching $4.4\times$ at an 83% prefix ratio, while suffix-dominated splits gain little; offloading dormant prefix activations lowers Phase-B peak HBM by up to 59% and extends trainable sequences by $1.66\times$.</p></details> | <details><summary>15 pages. Accepted to the 2026 ACM SIGOPS Annual T...</summary><p>15 pages. Accepted to the 2026 ACM SIGOPS Annual Technical Conference (ATC 2026)</p></details> |
| **[Kwai Summary Attention V2 Technical Report]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18654v2)** | 2026-10-15 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Summary-token architectures such as Kwai Summary Attention (KSA) compress distant context into learnable Summary token per chunk, and hybrid variants interleave these layers with full attention to retain exact access to the original text. In such hybrid KSA-Full architecture, the interleaving inserted summary tokens are served as a streaming flow role across different layers. Although effective, however, it also introduce some bottlenecks: (1) the different layers summary compression chunk must be same, therefore hard to reach a flexible KV Cache compression, e.g., different layer set different summary compression chunk window. (2) in the full-attention layers, the summary token introduced additional computation cost, but such layer ignore them and still pay quadratic prefilling, therefore unfriendly to the computation side. Motivated by them, we developed the KSA V2, which not only achieves a more flexible KV cache memory compression but also reduces the computation cost in Full attention layer. Specifically, we found that the summary tokens can serve two roles: the KV memory and sparse indexer.</p></details> | Work in progress |
| **[Augment the Cache, Replace the Activation: A 2x2 Study of Internal-State Sharing]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22026v1)** | 2026-10-15 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Multi-agent systems built from frozen language models communicate through text, which discards the internal state the sender already computed and makes the receiver pay to rebuild it. Work on internal channels avoids that cost, framing the problem as transfer: agent A sends information to agent B. Every agent pair that must communicate needs its own transfer bridge, and every agent added to a system needs a new bridge fitted against each previous agent. We reframe this problem as sharing: an agent publishes its internal state once into a pool, and every peer reads that pool through a single mechanism fitted to no sender in particular, so adding an agent adds a publisher and no new bridge. Whereas the carrier of the internal state and the fusion mechanism are usually chosen independently in the literature, our main finding is that these two choices are coupled; the deciding factor is where the carrier enters the receiver's computation. Consumability is a property of the receiving computation rather than of the representation. We find that the key-value (KV) cache must be augmented rather than swapped in: the receiver cross-attends over a peer's cache while keeping its own, and with only a small query-side adapter trained, matches the accuracy it gets from reading the source document. Activations invert this. They are best written straight into the receiver, with no bridge, no adapter and no training, which beats exposing them alongside the receiver's own, though that advantage rests on knowing where in the receiver the state belongs. The rule is augment the KV cache, replace the activation, established under one protocol with a shared control ladder. One adapter, trained once, also serves publishers it never trained on, and a pool of several at once, but only those whose internal state lies close to the receiver's own.</p></details> | 10 pages, 2 figures |
| **[Close Enough is Nowhere Near: Fidelity-Consumability Decoupling in KV Caches]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22016v1)** | 2026-10-15 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Multi-agent LLM systems communicate in text, which is lossy and wasteful: the sender throws away the reading it already did. A growing literature instead transmits the KV cache, the natural carrier of that reading. We study the most appealing form of the idea: both models stay frozen and the sender's cache is substituted for the reader's with nothing trained. It does not work, and the obstruction belongs to the reader. A frozen transformer reads only caches close to the one it would have written itself, a region we call its tolerable set. We show that geometric similarity to that cache does not predict whether the reader can use it, and the failure is not gradual, so a more faithful substitute is not the remedy it appears to be. We explain this phenomenon with competitive attention. Experimentally, we test eight diverse substitution methods against two measured anchors: an uninformative cache baseline and the reader's own accuracy from having read the passage. All sit at the baseline. That turns a long tail of separate negative results into one outcome with a stated condition for overturning it. A different design does work: if the reader keeps its own cache and attends over the sender's as extra context, adapting only its queries, it beats its own baseline, and also clears the baseline with eight senders pooled where undirected attention over the same union falls below it. For rules that reduce verifier rounds, accuracy typically drops substantially. Further analysis traces some failures to continued reasoning that exhausts the budget needed to deliver a final answer. | **[FlowCred: Hierarchical Credit Assignment and Functional Coordination for Joint Text-to-Video Post-Training]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18142v1)** | 2026-10-13 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Prompt optimization and generator post-training are two complementary ways to improve text-to-video (T2V) generation, and recent systems increasingly train both modules jointly. However, optimizing a prompt policy and a video generator from the same terminal reward creates two ambiguities: prompt quality is confounded with stochastic generation, and the two modules may realize overlapping local improvements. We introduce FlowCred, a two-level framework for joint T2V post-training. First, hierarchical credit assignment uses matched prompt-seed rollout grids to separate prompt-level credit from prompt-conditioned generator residuals under shared randomness. Second, functional coordination probes alternative current-policy prompts at states from actual generation trajectories, providing generator-aware evidence for prompt optimization while selectively attenuating generator updates already supported by conditioning changes. Across multiple T2V benchmarks, FlowCred consistently improves matched joint-training baselines. On LTX-2.5, FlowCred improves a strictly matched joint-training control from 61.47 to 64.46 on T2V-CompBench and from 55.58 to 58.08 on StoryEval, without increasing decoded-video or reward-model-call budgets. Factorial and realized-update analyses show complementary contributions from prompt shaping and generator routing, while human evaluation and transfer across backbones and updater families provide further supporting evidence.</p></details> |  |
| **[H-DDCM: Hadamard Codebooks for Fast Generative Image and Video Compression]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18125v1)** | 2026-10-13 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Training-free diffusion-based compression methods repurpose the generative priors of a diffusion or a flow model to compress data without retraining them as task-specific codecs. Recent codebook-based approaches such as Turbo-DDCM achieve strong perceptual quality at ultra-low bitrates, but their reliance on dense Gaussian codebooks remains costly in both memory and computation, and scales poorly with the large latent dimensions of modern image and video generators. Their combinatorial bitstream encoding further becomes computationally heavy at this scale. We introduce H-DDCM, a scalable generative compression framework that replaces Gaussian codebooks with implicit randomized Hadamard dictionaries. The fast Walsh-Hadamard transform allows for implicitly synthesizing full-dimensional dictionaries with $O(d \log d)$ compute for projection and reconstruction and $O(d)$ memory, without materializing the full-dimensional dictionary. We further introduce an efficient table-free lexicographic coding scheme that makes combinatorial encoding practical at larger dimensions. Beyond images, we adapt the framework to an autoregressive video flow model and develop a streaming compression scheme that periodically re-encodes recently reconstructed frames into a fresh KV-cache prefix, preserving temporal context across segments at no additional transmitted bits. This enables long-form, close to real-time generative video compression on a single GPU. Across image and video benchmarks, H-DDCM achieves competitive rate-distortion-perception performance while substantially reducing the memory and computational overhead of codebook-based training-free generative compression.</p></details> | <details><summary>Project's webpage at https://h-ddcm.github.io/...</summary><p>Project's webpage at https://h-ddcm.github.io/</p></details> |
| **[CineMem: Attention-Aligned Fine-grained Memory Retrieval for Multi-Shot Long Video Generation]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17926v1)** | 2026-10-13 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Autoregressive video generation relies on memory retrieval to model long-range dependencies. This capability becomes particularly critical for multi-shot generation, where models must reconcile substantial visual changes across shot transitions with persistent semantic continuity. Existing methods tend to perform memory retrieval at the frame level and share the same historical context across all query tokens, overlooking the heterogeneous information needs and leading to redundant retrieval and inefficient use of historical memory. To bridge this gap, we introduce CineMem, an attention-aligned fine-grained memory retrieval framework that combines online memory organization with query-adaptive retrieval for autoregressive multi-shot video generation. Specifically, guided by intrinsic memory-access patterns revealed through attention analysis, we propose an online-clustered KV cache as a memory organization strategy over all historical tokens, enabling semantic-aware memory grouping and more precise retrieval. In addition, we introduce a query-level retrieval mechanism that provides broader access to historical information under a fixed retrieval budget, thereby improving long-term memory utilization. Together, these designs enable the multi-shot video generator to preserve long-range consistency across shot transitions, particularly in revisitation scenarios, while approximating full-memory access under a constrained memory budget. To facilitate evaluation, we further introduce a suite of task-specific, VLM-assisted metrics for faithful inter-shot consistency assessment. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework.</p></details> | <details><summary>Project Page: https://uknowsth.github.io/CineMem/...</summary><p>Project Page: https://uknowsth.github.io/CineMem/</p></details> |
| **[Generative AI for Autonomous Driving: A Review]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15863v2)** | 2026-10-13 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Generative AI (GenAI) is rapidly advancing the field of Autonomous Driving (AD), extending beyond traditional applications in text, image, and video generation. We explore how generative models can enhance automotive tasks, such as static map creation, dynamic scenario generation, trajectory forecasting, and vehicle motion planning. By examining multiple generative approaches ranging from Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) and Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to Generative Transformers (GTs) and Diffusion Models (DMs), we highlight and compare their capabilities and limitations for AD-specific applications. Additionally, we discuss hybrid methods integrating conventional techniques with generative approaches, and emphasize their improved adaptability and robustness. We also identify relevant datasets and outline open research questions to guide future developments in GenAI. Finally, we discuss five core challenges: safety, interpretability, realtime capabilities, training and benchmarking. We also present recommendations for image generation, dynamic scenario generation, and planning.</p></details> | <details><summary>This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possi...</summary><p>This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication</p></details> |
| **[WeLike2Party! In-Context Motion Transfer for Multi-Human Image Animation]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36937v2)** | 2026-10-13 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Human image animation aims to transfer motion from a driving video to subjects in a reference image. To address this limitation, we propose WeLike2Party, a multi-human animation framework built on direct in-context video conditioning without explicit pose or mesh extraction at inference. We further introduce Reference Asymmetric RoPE Conditioning to preserve fine-grained appearance details, and Identity Binding Supervision to associate each reference identity with its intended motion trajectory. We additionally present MotionTwin-Bench, a cross-identity benchmark specifically designed to evaluate subject-level visual fidelity and identity-motion binding. Extensive experiments on MotionTwin-Bench and real-world videos demonstrate that WeLike2Party outperforms recent state-of-the-art methods in subject-level visual fidelity, identity-motion binding, and overall perceptual quality, particularly in multi-person interactions with substantial occlusion.</p></details> |  |
